title: You're the new hire
caption: Most of what you need to do the job well was never written down.
task: Plan next year’s summer party for 200 employees across Europe

questions.signoff: Who signs off on the plan?

hidden.label: The questions nobody thinks to ask
hidden.note: <marker>Context that even people forget to hand over, because it lives in feedback, in the culture or in habit rather than in any document</marker>.

questions.suppliers: Which tools and suppliers may I use?

handover.title: Now you hand it over.
handover.body: Your boss expects the plan by Friday, and the person taking over <marker>knows none of what you just learned</marker>.

why-the-middle-zone-stays-unwritten.header: Why the middle zone stays unwritten
why-the-middle-zone-stays-unwritten.description: Nonaka calls this tacit knowledge: "highly personal", "hard to formalize and, therefore, difficult to communicate to others"; in Polanyi's words, "We can know more than we can tell" [1].

nonaka-knowledge-creating-company.title: Ikujiro Nonaka, The Knowledge-Creating Company, Harvard Business Review (Nov-Dec 1991; reprinted as an HBR Classic, Jul-Aug 2007)

the-newcomer-has-the-least-to-absorb-wit.header: The newcomer has the least to absorb with
the-newcomer-has-the-least-to-absorb-wit.description: in 122 best-practice transfers between units in eight companies, knowledge-related barriers outweighed motivational ones; the recipient's lack of absorptive capacity weighed most (0.54), ahead of causal ambiguity (0.34) [1].

szulanski-internal-stickiness.title: Gabriel Szulanski, Exploring Internal Stickiness: Impediments to the Transfer of Best Practice Within the Firm, Strategic Management Journal 17 (1996)

even-the-experts-cannot-always-say-it.header: Even the experts cannot always say it
even-the-experts-cannot-always-say-it.description: a master baker's technique could not be read off X-rays of the dough; it took a developer's apprenticeship ("observation, imitation, and practice") and a year of trial and error before it was specified [1].

nonaka-knowledge-creating-company.title: Ikujiro Nonaka, The Knowledge-Creating Company, Harvard Business Review (Nov-Dec 1991; reprinted as an HBR Classic, Jul-Aug 2007)

one-caution-on-the-theory.description: Gourlay disputes Nonaka's account of knowledge being created by converting between tacit and explicit forms; the claim here rests on the definition of tacit knowledge, not on that conversion model [1].

gourlay-critique-of-nonaka.title: Stephen Gourlay, Conceptualizing Knowledge Creation: A Critique of Nonaka's Theory, Journal of Management Studies 43(7) (2006)

obvious-questions.title: Obvious questions
obvious-questions.script: Imagine you're a new hire. On day one, you get your first task: plan next year's summer party for all 200 employees across Europe. Your first questions are probably: what's the budget, where does everybody stay, who signs off? Maybe even dietary and accessibility needs.

the-ones-you-forget.title: The ones you forget
the-ones-you-forget.script: But the hard questions, the ones people usually don't think of but that matter just as much, are these: what went wrong last time, which unwritten rules apply (no paintball, for example), and which tools and suppliers are you allowed to use?

switch-of-roles.title: Switch of roles
switch-of-roles.script: Now let's switch roles. You're the one handing this task to a new hire on their first day. It's Monday, and the plan is due Friday. After everything we just went through, I think you realise you need to onboard that person with this context and these limitations, so they can work on it independently without knocking on your door every few minutes.
